questions.stem: A patient in cardiogenic shock has this chest radiograph. Which hemodynamic abnormality best explains the pulmonary findings shown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated right atrial pressure with clear lung fields

explanation.summary: The diffuse perihilar interstitial opacities represent pulmonary edema, which develops when elevated left-sided filling pressures (a high pulmonary capillary wedge pressure reflecting elevated left atrial pressure) force fluid into the alveoli. This is why IV fluids can worsen hypoxia in cardiogenic shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diffuse perihilar interstitial opacities represent pulmonary edema, which develops when elevated left-sided filling pressures (a high pulmonary capillary wedge pressure reflecting elevated left atrial pressure) force fluid into the alveoli. This is why IV fluids can worsen hypoxia in cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: This ECG rhythm strip shows beat-to-beat variation in QRS complex amplitude. This finding is most specific for which condition?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Large pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade

explanation.summary: The alternating high- and low-voltage QRS complexes are electrical alternans, produced by the swinging motion of the heart within a large fluid-filled pericardial sac. It is the most specific ECG finding for a large pericardial effusion causing tamponade.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alternating high- and low-voltage QRS complexes are electrical alternans, produced by the swinging motion of the heart within a large fluid-filled pericardial sac. It is the most specific ECG finding for a large pericardial effusion causing tamponade.

questions.stem: This chest radiograph was obtained from a hypotensive patient, and its findings are considered a contraindication to intravenous fluid administration. What abnormality does the film demonstrate?

explanation.summary: The radiograph shows engorged central pulmonary vessels and hazy interstitial markings characteristic of pulmonary edema. In a shock patient, radiographic pulmonary edema with hypoxia signals fluid overload, so IV fluids should be withheld rather than given.
explanation.whyCorrect: The radiograph shows engorged central pulmonary vessels and hazy interstitial markings characteristic of pulmonary edema. In a shock patient, radiographic pulmonary edema with hypoxia signals fluid overload, so IV fluids should be withheld rather than given.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows QRS complexes that alternate in amplitude from one beat to the next in a patient with a large pericardial effusion. What is the underlying cause of this finding?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alternating conduction block within the AV node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bundle branch block that alternates between beats

choices.label: D
choices.text: Swinging motion of the heart within the fluid-filled pericardial sac

explanation.summary: Electrical alternans is produced by the beat-to-beat 'swinging' of the heart as it moves back and forth within a large effusion, changing the QRS vector relative to the ECG electrodes. It is seen in a minority of tamponade patients and, with low-voltage QRS, suggests a large effusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Electrical alternans is produced by the beat-to-beat 'swinging' of the heart as it moves back and forth within a large effusion, changing the QRS vector relative to the ECG electrodes. It is seen in a minority of tamponade patients and, with low-voltage QRS, suggests a large effusion.

questions.stem: This schematic and paired echocardiogram demonstrate inward buckling of the right ventricular free wall during diastole. This early sign is most specific for which condition?

explanation.summary: Diastolic collapse of the low-pressure right ventricular free wall indicates that intrapericardial pressure is transiently exceeding RV filling pressure, an early echocardiographic sign of cardiac tamponade. The right-sided chambers collapse first because they operate at the lowest pressures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diastolic collapse of the low-pressure right ventricular free wall indicates that intrapericardial pressure is transiently exceeding RV filling pressure, an early echocardiographic sign of cardiac tamponade. The right-sided chambers collapse first because they operate at the lowest pressures.

questions.stem: This illustration shows a needle being advanced beneath the xiphoid toward the heart to aspirate fluid from around it. What is the name of this emergent procedure used to treat cardiac tamponade?

explanation.summary: Pericardiocentesis is percutaneous needle aspiration of fluid from the pericardial space, typically via a subxiphoid approach with a 16-18 gauge needle. It is the treatment of choice for relieving hemodynamic compromise in cardiac tamponade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pericardiocentesis is percutaneous needle aspiration of fluid from the pericardial space, typically via a subxiphoid approach with a 16-18 gauge needle. It is the treatment of choice for relieving hemodynamic compromise in cardiac tamponade.

questions.stem: In this color-Doppler echocardiogram of a patent ductus arteriosus, what does the bright mosaic (multicolored) signal at the pulmonary-artery end most likely represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Normal antegrade flow across the pulmonary valve

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turbulent, high-velocity shunt flow producing color aliasing

choices.label: E
choices.text: A calcified thrombus occluding the duct

explanation.summary: The high pressure gradient from aorta to pulmonary artery accelerates flow through the duct; the resulting turbulence exceeds the Nyquist limit and appears as a mosaic of aliased colors on Doppler.
explanation.whyCorrect: The high pressure gradient from aorta to pulmonary artery accelerates flow through the duct; the resulting turbulence exceeds the Nyquist limit and appears as a mosaic of aliased colors on Doppler.

questions.stem: This echocardiogram from a cyanotic neonate shows an aorta positioned above and straddling the interventricular septum, sitting over a septal defect. Which cyanotic congenital heart defect does this image represent?

explanation.summary: The echo demonstrates the overriding aorta and ventricular septal defect that are two of the four components of tetralogy of Fallot; the other two, pulmonary valve stenosis and RV hypertrophy, complete the tetrad.
explanation.whyCorrect: The echo demonstrates the overriding aorta and ventricular septal defect that are two of the four components of tetralogy of Fallot; the other two, pulmonary valve stenosis and RV hypertrophy, complete the tetrad.

questions.stem: This cardiac MR angiogram from an infant shows an enlarged right atrium, a markedly hypoplastic right ventricle, and no inlet from the RA to the RV. Which lesion does this represent?

explanation.summary: Absence of the tricuspid valve prevents RA-to-RV filling, so the RV receives little blood and becomes hypoplastic while the RA enlarges, the imaging hallmark of tricuspid atresia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Absence of the tricuspid valve prevents RA-to-RV filling, so the RV receives little blood and becomes hypoplastic while the RA enlarges, the imaging hallmark of tricuspid atresia.

questions.stem: This cardiac CT of the aortic root shows dense, bright white deposits (arrowheads) around the valve. What do these findings represent?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcification of the aortic valve and root

explanation.summary: On CT, calcium is markedly hyperdense (bright white). Cardiac CT is used to evaluate aortic stenosis because it clearly demonstrates the extent of valvular and root calcification, along with coronary anatomy (RCA, LCX, LAD).
explanation.whyCorrect: On CT, calcium is markedly hyperdense (bright white). Cardiac CT is used to evaluate aortic stenosis because it clearly demonstrates the extent of valvular and root calcification, along with coronary anatomy (RCA, LCX, LAD).

questions.stem: A clinician places the bell of a stethoscope over the antecubital fossa while inflating and slowly deflating an inflatable cuff around the upper arm, as shown. What auditory phenomenon is being used to determine the systolic and diastolic pressures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valvular closure clicks transmitted from the aortic valve

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pericardial friction rub amplified by cuff compression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Onset and disappearance of Korotkoff sounds as cuff pressure crosses arterial pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Venous hum produced by collapse of the brachial vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Continuous laminar flow murmur heard throughout deflation

explanation.summary: The sphygmomanometer cuff is inflated above systolic pressure to occlude the brachial artery; as it deflates, turbulent flow through the partially compressed artery produces Korotkoff sounds. The first sound marks systolic pressure and their disappearance marks diastolic pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sphygmomanometer cuff is inflated above systolic pressure to occlude the brachial artery; as it deflates, turbulent flow through the partially compressed artery produces Korotkoff sounds. The first sound marks systolic pressure and their disappearance marks diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: This 12-lead ECG shows a regular rhythm with a consistent 1:1 P-to-QRS relationship and normal waveform morphology at a notably slow rate. What is the underlying rhythm?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response

explanation.summary: A slow rate with an upright P wave preceding every QRS in a 1:1 fashion and normal PR interval indicates the impulse still originates in the SA node, defining sinus bradycardia rather than a junctional, blocked, or ectopic rhythm.
explanation.whyCorrect: A slow rate with an upright P wave preceding every QRS in a 1:1 fashion and normal PR interval indicates the impulse still originates in the SA node, defining sinus bradycardia rather than a junctional, blocked, or ectopic rhythm.

questions.stem: This ECG illustration counts the small boxes between two consecutive R waves to calculate heart rate. What calculation does this method use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Multiply the number of small boxes by 0.04 seconds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Divide 300 by the number of large boxes between R waves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Count QRS complexes in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10

choices.label: D
choices.text: Divide 60 by the R-R interval measured in large boxes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Divide 1500 by the number of small boxes between R waves

explanation.summary: The precise R-R small-box method divides 1500 (small boxes per minute at 25 mm/s) by the number of small boxes between consecutive R waves to yield beats per minute.
explanation.whyCorrect: The precise R-R small-box method divides 1500 (small boxes per minute at 25 mm/s) by the number of small boxes between consecutive R waves to yield beats per minute.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at roughly 130 bpm with a normal upright P wave preceding every QRS. What rhythm is this?

explanation.summary: A fast but regular rhythm with a normal P wave before each QRS and a constant PR interval indicates the SA node is simply firing faster, defining sinus tachycardia rather than a reentrant or ectopic tachyarrhythmia.
explanation.whyCorrect: A fast but regular rhythm with a normal P wave before each QRS and a constant PR interval indicates the SA node is simply firing faster, defining sinus tachycardia rather than a reentrant or ectopic tachyarrhythmia.

questions.stem: This magnetic resonance angiogram shows lack of contrast filling of the right renal artery at its branch point from the aorta in an older diabetic patient. What is the most likely underlying cause?

explanation.summary: In older patients, especially those with diabetes and other atherosclerotic risk factors, renal artery stenosis is usually caused by atherosclerotic plaque near the ostium, reducing renal blood flow and activating the RAAS to cause secondary hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: In older patients, especially those with diabetes and other atherosclerotic risk factors, renal artery stenosis is usually caused by atherosclerotic plaque near the ostium, reducing renal blood flow and activating the RAAS to cause secondary hypertension.

questions.stem: This renal arteriogram demonstrates a characteristic 'string of beads' appearance of the artery. This finding is diagnostic of which condition?

explanation.summary: The alternating stenosis and aneurysmal dilation producing a 'string of beads' pattern is the classic angiographic hallmark of fibromuscular dysplasia, most often seen in young women and a treatable cause of secondary hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alternating stenosis and aneurysmal dilation producing a 'string of beads' pattern is the classic angiographic hallmark of fibromuscular dysplasia, most often seen in young women and a treatable cause of secondary hypertension.

questions.stem: The upper tracing contrasts a murmur with the mitral stenosis pattern below it. What is the timing and shape of the upper murmur?

explanation.summary: Aortic regurgitation produces a soft, high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur that begins right after S2, when the aortic-to-LV pressure gradient is greatest and then falls. Mitral stenosis instead gives a mid-to-late diastolic rumble.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aortic regurgitation produces a soft, high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur that begins right after S2, when the aortic-to-LV pressure gradient is greatest and then falls. Mitral stenosis instead gives a mid-to-late diastolic rumble.

questions.stem: Compared with the normal fundus on the left, the right fundoscopic image from a hypertensive patient shows a swollen optic disc with blurred margins and engorged vessels. What does the abnormal finding indicate?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raised intracranial pressure transmitted to the optic nerve head

choices.label: E
choices.text: Occlusion of the central retinal artery

explanation.summary: The bulging disc with blurred margins and engorged veins is papilledema, reflecting elevated intracranial pressure from cerebral edema in hypertensive emergency, not an arterial occlusion, diabetic, detachment, or atrophic process.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bulging disc with blurred margins and engorged veins is papilledema, reflecting elevated intracranial pressure from cerebral edema in hypertensive emergency, not an arterial occlusion, diabetic, detachment, or atrophic process.

questions.stem: This clinician is palpating deeply in the mid-abdomen above the umbilicus in a patient with suspected aortic aneurysm. What physical finding is being sought?

explanation.summary: A pulsatile, expansile mass palpated above the umbilicus suggests an AAA; below that level the aorta has bifurcated into the common iliac arteries.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pulsatile, expansile mass palpated above the umbilicus suggests an AAA; below that level the aorta has bifurcated into the common iliac arteries.

questions.stem: Bedside ultrasound is preferred over CT for a hypotensive patient with a suspected ruptured AAA primarily because it:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Can be performed at the bedside without transporting an unstable patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: Has higher spatial resolution than CT

choices.label: E
choices.text: Better visualizes the retroperitoneum than CT

explanation.summary: In an unstable, hypotensive patient, point-of-care ultrasound rapidly confirms an aneurysm at the bedside, avoiding the risk of transporting the patient to the radiology department.
explanation.whyCorrect: In an unstable, hypotensive patient, point-of-care ultrasound rapidly confirms an aneurysm at the bedside, avoiding the risk of transporting the patient to the radiology department.

questions.stem: CT angiography is considered the gold-standard imaging modality for evaluating an aortic aneurysm chiefly because it is the most effective tool for:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Detailed anatomic assessment and pre-operative planning

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bedside evaluation of an unstable, hypotensive patient

choices.label: C
choices.text: Avoiding the need for IV contrast

explanation.summary: CT angiography provides the detailed anatomy needed for pre-operative planning in stable patients; the hypotensive patient is more safely evaluated with bedside ultrasound.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT angiography provides the detailed anatomy needed for pre-operative planning in stable patients; the hypotensive patient is more safely evaluated with bedside ultrasound.

questions.stem: This chest X-ray finding was discovered incidentally in a patient later found to have a thoracic aortic aneurysm. Such an aneurysm can also compress an adjacent nerve, producing which symptom?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve compression

explanation.summary: A thoracic aortic aneurysm may show mediastinal widening on X-ray and can compress the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness, or compress the trachea/esophagus.
explanation.whyCorrect: A thoracic aortic aneurysm may show mediastinal widening on X-ray and can compress the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness, or compress the trachea/esophagus.

questions.stem: This CT shows an abdominal aortic aneurysm surrounded by inflammatory change with pockets of gas (black foci) in the wall. What does the presence of gas indicate?

explanation.summary: Periaortic inflammation with gas points to an infected (mycotic) aneurysm; these are rare but life-threatening and require prompt antibiotics plus surgical resection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Periaortic inflammation with gas points to an infected (mycotic) aneurysm; these are rare but life-threatening and require prompt antibiotics plus surgical resection.

questions.stem: This contrast-enhanced axial chest image of a stable patient shows the aorta divided into two channels separated by a thin line. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: The CT angiogram shows an intimal flap separating a true and false lumen, which is diagnostic of aortic dissection. CT angiography is the preferred imaging modality in hemodynamically stable patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The CT angiogram shows an intimal flap separating a true and false lumen, which is diagnostic of aortic dissection. CT angiography is the preferred imaging modality in hemodynamically stable patients.

questions.stem: This ultrasound image was obtained at the bedside using a probe passed through the esophagus, revealing an intimal flap within the aorta. Which imaging modality is this?

explanation.summary: This is a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE), preferred in hemodynamically unstable patients because it can be performed rapidly at the bedside and clearly demonstrates the intimal flap separating the true and false lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE), preferred in hemodynamically unstable patients because it can be performed rapidly at the bedside and clearly demonstrates the intimal flap separating the true and false lumen.

questions.stem: This duplex ultrasound of the temporal artery shows a dark hypoechoic ring surrounding the flowing vessel lumen. What does this characteristic 'halo' represent?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Edema and thickening of the inflamed arterial wall

explanation.summary: The halo sign is a hypoechoic rim around the lumen produced by inflammatory wall thickening and edema, a supportive imaging finding for GCA (sensitivity ~87%, specificity ~96%). It reflects mural inflammation, not calcium, thrombus, or infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The halo sign is a hypoechoic rim around the lumen produced by inflammatory wall thickening and edema, a supportive imaging finding for GCA (sensitivity ~87%, specificity ~96%). It reflects mural inflammation, not calcium, thrombus, or infection.

questions.stem: This MR angiogram (brackets) of a young woman demonstrates narrowing of the aorta and its branches. Which pattern of stenosis, characteristic of this disease, distinguishes it from atherosclerotic disease?

explanation.summary: Takayasu arteritis produces long, smooth, tapered segments of stenosis (the 'macaroni sign'), often with an undulating pattern. Atherosclerotic stenosis is instead nonhomogeneous, irregular, and involves shorter segments; the string-of-beads pattern typifies fibromuscular dysplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Takayasu arteritis produces long, smooth, tapered segments of stenosis (the 'macaroni sign'), often with an undulating pattern. Atherosclerotic stenosis is instead nonhomogeneous, irregular, and involves shorter segments; the string-of-beads pattern typifies fibromuscular dysplasia.

questions.stem: This mesenteric angiogram from a patient with polyarteritis nodosa shows multiple small outpouchings (red arrows) in a 'beads-on-a-string' pattern. These beads represent which lesion?

explanation.summary: PAN is a segmental disease with alternating aneurysms and strictures. The 'beads' on angiography are small arterial microaneurysms, a characteristic diagnostic finding.
explanation.whyCorrect: PAN is a segmental disease with alternating aneurysms and strictures. The 'beads' on angiography are small arterial microaneurysms, a characteristic diagnostic finding.

questions.stem: This funduscopic image shows a pale optic region with a cherry-red spot at the macula and cotton-wool spots. What vascular event does this appearance indicate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery

explanation.summary: A pale, edematous retina with a cherry-red macula and cotton-wool spots on funduscopy is the classic picture of central retinal artery occlusion from an embolus, in which the thin foveal retina still perfused by the choroid appears red against the surrounding ischemic pallor.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pale, edematous retina with a cherry-red macula and cotton-wool spots on funduscopy is the classic picture of central retinal artery occlusion from an embolus, in which the thin foveal retina still perfused by the choroid appears red against the surrounding ischemic pallor.

questions.stem: This contrast-enhanced CT angiogram uses arrows to mark filling defects in paired abdominal organs' arterial supply. Which imaging modality is depicted and why is it preferred here?

choices.label: A
choices.text: MRI without contrast, because it best resolves cholesterol crystals

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conventional radiography, because it is fastest for bony detail

choices.label: C
choices.text: Duplex ultrasound, because it avoids radiation exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-contrast CT, because it best highlights soft-tissue calcification

choices.label: E
choices.text: CT angiography, because it shows both the site and degree of arterial occlusion

explanation.summary: CT angiography is the imaging modality of choice for arterial thromboembolism: injected contrast opacifies patent branches so that occlusions (here, bilateral renal artery emboli marked by arrows) are seen as filling defects, revealing both location and degree of obstruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT angiography is the imaging modality of choice for arterial thromboembolism: injected contrast opacifies patent branches so that occlusions (here, bilateral renal artery emboli marked by arrows) are seen as filling defects, revealing both location and degree of obstruction.

questions.stem: On this non-contrast head CT, the red arrow points to an ill-defined area of decreased attenuation in the right hemisphere. What does this finding most likely represent?

choices.label: B
choices.text: An acute ischemic infarct in the middle cerebral artery territory

explanation.summary: Loss of gray-white differentiation and hypodensity mark an evolving ischemic infarct; here an embolus of carotid origin has occluded the right middle cerebral artery. Hemorrhage would appear hyperdense (bright).
explanation.whyCorrect: Loss of gray-white differentiation and hypodensity mark an evolving ischemic infarct; here an embolus of carotid origin has occluded the right middle cerebral artery. Hemorrhage would appear hyperdense (bright).

questions.stem: The technique illustrated uses inflatable cuffs and an ultrasound probe to record systolic pressures at the arm and the ankle. Comparing these two pressures yields which diagnostic value used to assess peripheral arterial disease?

explanation.summary: Dividing the systolic pressure at the ankle by the systolic pressure at the brachial artery gives the ankle-brachial index (ABI). Normally ankle pressure exceeds brachial pressure; in PAD ankle pressure falls, lowering the ratio, with values under 1.0 abnormal and under 0.4 indicating severe disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dividing the systolic pressure at the ankle by the systolic pressure at the brachial artery gives the ankle-brachial index (ABI). Normally ankle pressure exceeds brachial pressure; in PAD ankle pressure falls, lowering the ratio, with values under 1.0 abnormal and under 0.4 indicating severe disease.

questions.stem: In the bedside maneuver shown, the suspected limb is gradually raised while supine and observed for color change. Development of pallor at a low elevation angle indicates what?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inadequate arterial perfusion of the limb

explanation.summary: A healthy leg stays pink even at 90 degrees, but in PAD the leg blanches at a lower angle because gravity overcomes the compromised arterial pressure; the more severe the disease, the smaller the vascular angle at which pallor appears (as low as 15 degrees).
explanation.whyCorrect: A healthy leg stays pink even at 90 degrees, but in PAD the leg blanches at a lower angle because gravity overcomes the compromised arterial pressure; the more severe the disease, the smaller the vascular angle at which pallor appears (as low as 15 degrees).

questions.stem: This high-resolution coronary CT angiogram is annotated with a white arrow pointing to the left anterior descending artery. What does the arrow indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A myocardial bridge over a normal vessel

choices.label: D
choices.text: A saccular aneurysm of the vessel

explanation.summary: Coronary CT angiography is a sensitive noninvasive test for coronary artery occlusion. The arrow marks a focal narrowing (stenosis) of the LAD lumen; a positive scan is typically confirmed with functional testing or invasive angiography before intervention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coronary CT angiography is a sensitive noninvasive test for coronary artery occlusion. The arrow marks a focal narrowing (stenosis) of the LAD lumen; a positive scan is typically confirmed with functional testing or invasive angiography before intervention.

questions.stem: This graph plots cardiac biomarker levels (as multiples of the upper limit of normal) over the days following MI onset. Approximately how many hours after onset do these markers first become detectable in the serum?

explanation.summary: Cardiac biomarkers such as troponin and CK-MB become detectable roughly 4-6 hours after MI onset. Because a test may therefore be falsely negative on early arrival at the ER, the ECG remains the best initial test and serial biomarker testing is required.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiac biomarkers such as troponin and CK-MB become detectable roughly 4-6 hours after MI onset. Because a test may therefore be falsely negative on early arrival at the ER, the ECG remains the best initial test and serial biomarker testing is required.

questions.stem: This 12-lead ECG shows ST-segment elevation concentrated in leads V2 through V6 along with I and aVL. Occlusion of which coronary artery does this pattern most likely represent?

explanation.summary: ST elevation across the precordial leads with lateral involvement (I, aVL) defines an anterolateral injury pattern, which corresponds to the left coronary system, chiefly the LAD and its branches. RCA occlusion instead produces inferior (II, III, aVF) changes.
explanation.whyCorrect: ST elevation across the precordial leads with lateral involvement (I, aVL) defines an anterolateral injury pattern, which corresponds to the left coronary system, chiefly the LAD and its branches. RCA occlusion instead produces inferior (II, III, aVF) changes.

questions.stem: This 12-lead ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal depression in lead aVL. Which myocardial territory is undergoing acute injury?

explanation.summary: ST elevation in the inferior lead group (II, III, aVF) with reciprocal ST depression in aVL localizes the injury to the inferior wall, most often from right coronary artery occlusion. Anterior injury would elevate the precordial leads instead.
explanation.whyCorrect: ST elevation in the inferior lead group (II, III, aVF) with reciprocal ST depression in aVL localizes the injury to the inferior wall, most often from right coronary artery occlusion. Anterior injury would elevate the precordial leads instead.

questions.stem: This illustration adds three electrodes wrapping toward the back of the left thorax, shown with the underlying heart, to extend the standard recording. Infarction of which myocardial wall are these back-positioned leads placed to detect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The posterior wall of the left ventricle

explanation.summary: Leads V7-V9 are placed around the left posterior thorax to record directly over the posterior left ventricle, where standard leads show only subtle reciprocal changes. They are used to confirm acute posterior infarction, often from right coronary or left circumflex territory occlusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leads V7-V9 are placed around the left posterior thorax to record directly over the posterior left ventricle, where standard leads show only subtle reciprocal changes. They are used to confirm acute posterior infarction, often from right coronary or left circumflex territory occlusion.

questions.stem: In this paired coronary angiogram, panel A shows an inferior-wall STEMI patient with an arrow marking an abrupt cutoff of contrast in the right coronary artery, and panel B is obtained after intervention. What does panel A most likely demonstrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete thrombotic occlusion of the right coronary artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal, fully patent right coronary artery

explanation.summary: The arrow marks an abrupt termination of the contrast column with no distal filling, indicating total occlusion of the right coronary artery causing the inferior STEMI. Panel B shows restored antegrade contrast (normal perfusion) after percutaneous coronary intervention.
explanation.whyCorrect: The arrow marks an abrupt termination of the contrast column with no distal filling, indicating total occlusion of the right coronary artery causing the inferior STEMI. Panel B shows restored antegrade contrast (normal perfusion) after percutaneous coronary intervention.

questions.stem: The circled fibrin degradation fragment produced as this crosslinked clot breaks down is measured by a blood test that has which diagnostic property for DVT?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both highly sensitive and highly specific

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diagnostic only when combined with a bleeding time

explanation.summary: D-dimer, a fibrin degradation product, is elevated in many conditions; it is sensitive but not specific, so a normal value helps rule out DVT while an elevation is nonspecific.
explanation.whyCorrect: D-dimer, a fibrin degradation product, is elevated in many conditions; it is sensitive but not specific, so a normal value helps rule out DVT while an elevation is nonspecific.

questions.stem: In this paired before- and with-compression ultrasound of a leg vein, the vein that fails to collapse under external pressure indicates what?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Presence of a deep vein thrombosis

explanation.summary: A normal vein collapses with compression; a vein that stays open when pressure is applied signals an intraluminal clot, the diagnostic finding for DVT on compression ultrasonography.
explanation.whyCorrect: A normal vein collapses with compression; a vein that stays open when pressure is applied signals an intraluminal clot, the diagnostic finding for DVT on compression ultrasonography.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip was recorded in a patient on a Class IA antiarrhythmic with a prolonged QT interval. What is this arrhythmia?

explanation.summary: The strip shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that twist around the baseline, the hallmark of torsades de pointes, a complication of QT prolongation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The strip shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that twist around the baseline, the hallmark of torsades de pointes, a complication of QT prolongation.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows a regular rhythm at a rate of approximately 43 bpm with an upright P wave of normal morphology preceding every narrow QRS complex. What rhythm does this represent?

explanation.summary: A regular rhythm below 60 bpm with a normal P wave preceding each QRS (normal PR interval and axis) indicates the impulse originates from the SA node at a slow rate, defining sinus bradycardia. A junctional rhythm would lack normal preceding P waves, and atrial fibrillation would be irregular with no discrete P waves.
explanation.whyCorrect: A regular rhythm below 60 bpm with a normal P wave preceding each QRS (normal PR interval and axis) indicates the impulse originates from the SA node at a slow rate, defining sinus bradycardia. A junctional rhythm would lack normal preceding P waves, and atrial fibrillation would be irregular with no discrete P waves.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip demonstrates narrow QRS complexes without preceding P waves at a rate of roughly 40-60 bpm. What rhythm is shown?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete heart block with ventricular escape

explanation.summary: When the SA node fails or is severely slowed, the AV junction acts as a subsidiary pacemaker firing at ~40-60 bpm. Because impulses travel down the normal His-Purkinje system the QRS is narrow, and P waves are absent (or inverted near the QRS) because there is no normal atrial depolarization from the SA node.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the SA node fails or is severely slowed, the AV junction acts as a subsidiary pacemaker firing at ~40-60 bpm. Because impulses travel down the normal His-Purkinje system the QRS is narrow, and P waves are absent (or inverted near the QRS) because there is no normal atrial depolarization from the SA node.

questions.stem: This tracing demonstrates a coarse fibrillatory baseline (best appreciated in lead V1) together with an irregularly irregular QRS response. What is the approximate atrial depolarization rate characteristic of this rhythm?

explanation.summary: In atrial fibrillation, multiple simultaneous reentrant wavelets produce a chaotic atrial rate exceeding 350 per minute. The AV node filters these impulses irregularly, producing the irregularly irregular ventricular response seen here.
explanation.whyCorrect: In atrial fibrillation, multiple simultaneous reentrant wavelets produce a chaotic atrial rate exceeding 350 per minute. The AV node filters these impulses irregularly, producing the irregularly irregular ventricular response seen here.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows a beat whose P wave arrives early and has a different shape from the preceding sinus P waves, yet is followed by a normal narrow QRS. Which arrhythmia does this tracing best represent?

explanation.summary: An early, abnormally shaped (ectopic) P wave that is still conducted through the AV node to produce a normal narrow QRS is the hallmark of a premature atrial contraction. A PVC would show a wide QRS with no preceding P wave.
explanation.whyCorrect: An early, abnormally shaped (ectopic) P wave that is still conducted through the AV node to produce a normal narrow QRS is the hallmark of a premature atrial contraction. A PVC would show a wide QRS with no preceding P wave.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows organized sawtooth atrial waves at a constant rate, but the spacing between QRS complexes varies from beat to beat. What accounts for the irregular ventricular response seen here?

explanation.summary: In atrial flutter the atrial (flutter) rate is fixed; when the AV node conducts at changing ratios (e.g. alternating 2:1 and 4:1) the ventricular rhythm becomes irregular even though the atrial rate is constant.
explanation.whyCorrect: In atrial flutter the atrial (flutter) rate is fixed; when the AV node conducts at changing ratios (e.g. alternating 2:1 and 4:1) the ventricular rhythm becomes irregular even though the atrial rate is constant.

questions.stem: This ECG from a patient with chronic lung disease shows an irregular tachycardia in which the P waves (arrows) have at least three distinct shapes. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Three or more distinct P-wave morphologies with an irregular rate over 100/min define multifocal atrial tachycardia, seen most often with pulmonary disease. Atrial fibrillation lacks discrete organized P waves.
explanation.whyCorrect: Three or more distinct P-wave morphologies with an irregular rate over 100/min define multifocal atrial tachycardia, seen most often with pulmonary disease. Atrial fibrillation lacks discrete organized P waves.

questions.stem: This ECG shows an abrupt regular narrow-complex tachycardia in which a retrograde P wave is buried just after each QRS. In young, otherwise healthy patients this rhythm is most commonly caused by which mechanism?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reentry through dual AV nodal pathways

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reentry over an accessory bypass tract

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhanced automaticity of an atrial focus

explanation.summary: AVNRT is a micro-reentrant circuit using fast and slow pathways within the AV node, producing a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with a retrograde P wave close to the QRS. It is the most common SVT in young people.
explanation.whyCorrect: AVNRT is a micro-reentrant circuit using fast and slow pathways within the AV node, producing a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with a retrograde P wave close to the QRS. It is the most common SVT in young people.

questions.stem: This schematic contrasts a normal QRS with one that has a slurred upstroke at its onset and a shortened PR interval. What underlying electrophysiologic event produces this waveform change?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ventricular pre-excitation via an accessory pathway

explanation.summary: The slurred initial upstroke (delta wave) with a short PR interval reflects early ventricular depolarization arriving through an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node, i.e. pre-excitation as in WPW.
explanation.whyCorrect: The slurred initial upstroke (delta wave) with a short PR interval reflects early ventricular depolarization arriving through an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node, i.e. pre-excitation as in WPW.

questions.stem: This baseline (sinus rhythm) 12-lead ECG shows a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS complexes (arrows). What does this finding indicate?

choices.label: D
choices.text: An accessory conduction pathway is present

explanation.summary: The short PR interval plus delta waves during sinus rhythm signify ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory (Kent) bundle, the defining ECG signature of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The short PR interval plus delta waves during sinus rhythm signify ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory (Kent) bundle, the defining ECG signature of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows every P wave followed by a QRS, but with a uniformly prolonged interval from the start of P to the start of QRS (>200 ms). What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: First-degree AV block is defined by a fixed PR interval greater than 0.2 s with every atrial impulse conducted to the ventricles; no beats are dropped, so it is purely an ECG finding and usually asymptomatic.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-degree AV block is defined by a fixed PR interval greater than 0.2 s with every atrial impulse conducted to the ventricles; no beats are dropped, so it is purely an ECG finding and usually asymptomatic.

questions.stem: This tracing shows the PR interval progressively lengthening over consecutive beats until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle repeats. What does it depict?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block

explanation.summary: Wenckebach (Mobitz I) shows progressive PR prolongation of consecutively conducted beats until one P wave fails to conduct and a QRS is dropped; the block is typically within the AV node and usually benign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Wenckebach (Mobitz I) shows progressive PR prolongation of consecutively conducted beats until one P wave fails to conduct and a QRS is dropped; the block is typically within the AV node and usually benign.

questions.stem: This tracing shows constant PR intervals of conducted beats with a sudden non-conducted P wave (dropped QRS) and no preceding PR lengthening. What does it depict?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block

explanation.summary: Mobitz type II shows a fixed PR interval in conducted beats followed by an abrupt non-conducted P wave. The block is usually below the AV node (His-Purkinje), is intrinsic/chronic, and frequently progresses to complete heart block, so it warrants a pacemaker.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mobitz type II shows a fixed PR interval in conducted beats followed by an abrupt non-conducted P wave. The block is usually below the AV node (His-Purkinje), is intrinsic/chronic, and frequently progresses to complete heart block, so it warrants a pacemaker.

questions.stem: This strip shows regular P waves and regular QRS complexes marching at independent rates with no fixed relationship between them. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: In complete heart block there is no conduction between atria and ventricles; P waves and QRS complexes are dissociated, each with its own rate (P faster than QRS), and a slow escape pacemaker drives the ventricles.
explanation.whyCorrect: In complete heart block there is no conduction between atria and ventricles; P waves and QRS complexes are dissociated, each with its own rate (P faster than QRS), and a slow escape pacemaker drives the ventricles.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with dizziness. This ECG shows two P waves for every QRS with a fixed, dangerously slow ventricular rate (~43/min); labs, ABGs and chest x-ray are normal and he is on no medications. What is the best management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals

explanation.summary: This is a fixed 2:1 AV block with a symptomatic, dangerously slow ventricular rate and no reversible cause (no drugs, electrolyte disturbance, or acute MI). A symptomatic, irreversible high-grade block is an indication for permanent pacing.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is a fixed 2:1 AV block with a symptomatic, dangerously slow ventricular rate and no reversible cause (no drugs, electrolyte disturbance, or acute MI). A symptomatic, irreversible high-grade block is an indication for permanent pacing.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows each normal sinus beat regularly alternating with a single premature, wide-QRS beat of ventricular origin. What is this repeating pattern called?

explanation.summary: When every other beat is a premature ventricular contraction (a normal beat coupled to one PVC in a 1:1 repeating sequence), the pattern is termed ventricular bigeminy. Trigeminy would be every third beat, and a couplet is two consecutive PVCs.
explanation.whyCorrect: When every other beat is a premature ventricular contraction (a normal beat coupled to one PVC in a 1:1 repeating sequence), the pattern is termed ventricular bigeminy. Trigeminy would be every third beat, and a couplet is two consecutive PVCs.

questions.stem: This continuous rhythm strip shows a chaotic polymorphic ventricular arrhythmia that is abruptly interrupted midway by a high-energy therapy, after which organized rhythm resumes. What device delivered this therapy?

explanation.summary: The abrupt in-strip termination of a life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia by an internally delivered shock is the signature of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator sensing and treating the rhythm automatically.
explanation.whyCorrect: The abrupt in-strip termination of a life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia by an internally delivered shock is the signature of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator sensing and treating the rhythm automatically.

questions.stem: This ECG shows a rapid, regular, wide-QRS rhythm with uniform beat-to-beat complex morphology and no clearly related P waves. What is the arrhythmia?

explanation.summary: A fast, regular series of wide QRS complexes that all share the same shape (monomorphic) with AV dissociation indicates monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, distinct from the varying complexes of polymorphic VT and the chaotic disorganization of VF.
explanation.whyCorrect: A fast, regular series of wide QRS complexes that all share the same shape (monomorphic) with AV dissociation indicates monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, distinct from the varying complexes of polymorphic VT and the chaotic disorganization of VF.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows continuous chaotic, irregular oscillations of varying amplitude with no identifiable QRS complexes and no organized electrical activity. What is the arrhythmia?

explanation.summary: The absence of any organized QRS complexes, replaced by disorganized fibrillatory waves reflecting uncoordinated quivering of the ventricular myocardium with no effective cardiac output, is diagnostic of ventricular fibrillation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The absence of any organized QRS complexes, replaced by disorganized fibrillatory waves reflecting uncoordinated quivering of the ventricular myocardium with no effective cardiac output, is diagnostic of ventricular fibrillation.

questions.stem: A clinician presses on the swollen lower legs shown and the skin retains a lasting indentation. This physical finding is most characteristically associated with which category of disease?

explanation.summary: The lasting indentation identifies pitting edema, which reflects excess mobile interstitial fluid and is classically linked to cardiac, hepatic, or renal disease. Myxedema is nonpitting, angioedema and cellulitis are localized and acute, and lymphatic obstruction tends to produce nonpitting lymphedema.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lasting indentation identifies pitting edema, which reflects excess mobile interstitial fluid and is classically linked to cardiac, hepatic, or renal disease. Myxedema is nonpitting, angioedema and cellulitis are localized and acute, and lymphatic obstruction tends to produce nonpitting lymphedema.

questions.stem: The ECG tracing shown, paired with the depicted myocardial change, meets diagnostic voltage criteria. What anatomic abnormality produces the high-amplitude QRS complexes in the lateral leads?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased left ventricular muscle mass (left ventricular hypertrophy)

choices.label: C
choices.text: A left bundle branch conduction delay

explanation.summary: The diagram shows a thickened left ventricle and the ECG shows tall QRS complexes. Increased LV mass generates a larger electrical signal, producing high-voltage QRS complexes in the lateral leads that meet voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, often with a lateral strain pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram shows a thickened left ventricle and the ECG shows tall QRS complexes. Increased LV mass generates a larger electrical signal, producing high-voltage QRS complexes in the lateral leads that meet voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, often with a lateral strain pattern.

questions.stem: This chest radiograph is from a patient with left heart failure following a myocardial infarction. What do the fluffy, symmetric perihilar opacities most likely represent?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pulmonary edema from elevated pulmonary venous hydrostatic pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: A wedge-shaped infarct from pulmonary embolism

explanation.summary: Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary venous and capillary pressure, forcing fluid into the interstitium and alveoli. On chest X-ray this appears as symmetric perihilar (bat-wing) opacities with vascular redistribution, characteristic of cardiogenic pulmonary edema rather than the focal consolidation of pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary venous and capillary pressure, forcing fluid into the interstitium and alveoli. On chest X-ray this appears as symmetric perihilar (bat-wing) opacities with vascular redistribution, characteristic of cardiogenic pulmonary edema rather than the focal consolidation of pneumonia.

questions.stem: This echocardiogram is from a patient who uses injectable drugs. The mobile echodensity indicated on the valve most likely represents which of the following?

choices.label: D
choices.text: A bland thrombus from atrial fibrillation

choices.label: E
choices.text: A Libman-Sacks vegetation of systemic lupus erythematosus

explanation.summary: Injection drug use delivers bacteria directly into the venous blood, and the tricuspid valve is the first valve these organisms encounter, making right-sided infective endocarditis common. The echo shows a vegetation on the tricuspid valve projecting into the right ventricle, adjacent to the right atrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Injection drug use delivers bacteria directly into the venous blood, and the tricuspid valve is the first valve these organisms encounter, making right-sided infective endocarditis common. The echo shows a vegetation on the tricuspid valve projecting into the right ventricle, adjacent to the right atrium.

questions.stem: This illustration depicts a needle being advanced at an angle toward the sac surrounding the heart. This procedure is most urgently indicated in which clinical scenario?

explanation.summary: Pericardiocentesis drains pericardial fluid and is urgently indicated for cardiac tamponade or when purulent pericarditis is suspected.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pericardiocentesis drains pericardial fluid and is urgently indicated for cardiac tamponade or when purulent pericarditis is suspected.

questions.stem: This echocardiogram and accompanying schematic demonstrate collapse of the right ventricular free wall during ventricular diastole in cardiac tamponade. Why is this chamber affected earliest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the last chamber to contract in the cardiac cycle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It lies farthest from the pericardial surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has the thickest myocardial wall of the four chambers

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a low-pressure chamber, so rising intrapericardial pressure exceeds its filling pressure first

choices.label: E
choices.text: It generates the highest systolic pressure in the heart

explanation.summary: As intrapericardial pressure rises it first overcomes the pressure in the lowest-pressure chamber. The right ventricle fills at low diastolic pressures, so its free wall collapses in diastole before the higher-pressure left-sided chambers, making this an early echocardiographic sign of tamponade.
explanation.whyCorrect: As intrapericardial pressure rises it first overcomes the pressure in the lowest-pressure chamber. The right ventricle fills at low diastolic pressures, so its free wall collapses in diastole before the higher-pressure left-sided chambers, making this an early echocardiographic sign of tamponade.

questions.stem: This illustration shows a needle being advanced at roughly 45 degrees below the xiphoid toward the sac surrounding the heart. What is the purpose of the procedure depicted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspiration of fluid from the pericardial space to relieve tamponade

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biopsy of the myocardium for suspected myocarditis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placement of a transvenous pacemaker lead

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intracoronary injection of a thrombolytic agent

explanation.summary: The image depicts pericardiocentesis: percutaneous needle aspiration of pericardial fluid via a subxiphoid approach angled toward the pericardial sac. It is the emergent treatment for cardiac tamponade, removing fluid to restore diastolic filling.
explanation.whyCorrect: The image depicts pericardiocentesis: percutaneous needle aspiration of pericardial fluid via a subxiphoid approach angled toward the pericardial sac. It is the emergent treatment for cardiac tamponade, removing fluid to restore diastolic filling.

questions.stem: This 12-lead ECG from a patient with sharp chest pain that improves on sitting up and leaning forward demonstrates the labeled changes across multiple leads. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression across multiple leads (rather than a single vascular territory) is the classic ECG signature of acute pericarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression across multiple leads (rather than a single vascular territory) is the classic ECG signature of acute pericarditis.

questions.stem: This cross-sectional CT/MR angiographic image (arrow) provides a 3D picture used to plan intervention for which aortic abnormality?

explanation.summary: CT and MR imaging give a detailed 3D depiction of the narrowed segment and associated anatomic abnormalities of aortic coarctation, aiding planning of the appropriate intervention.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT and MR imaging give a detailed 3D depiction of the narrowed segment and associated anatomic abnormalities of aortic coarctation, aiding planning of the appropriate intervention.

questions.stem: These sequential catheter angiograms show a coarctation before treatment (left), during the procedure (middle), and after the procedure (right). Which intervention is depicted?

explanation.summary: Transcatheter intervention with placement of a percutaneous stent across the narrowed segment is the preferred approach in older children and adults with coarctation of the aorta.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transcatheter intervention with placement of a percutaneous stent across the narrowed segment is the preferred approach in older children and adults with coarctation of the aorta.

questions.stem: This cardiac image uses the colored overlay between the aorta and pulmonary artery to detect and grade a ductal shunt. Which imaging technique produces this colored signal?

explanation.summary: The mosaic color mapped onto the grayscale ultrasound is color Doppler, which encodes blood flow direction and velocity. It reveals the turbulent shunt jet of a patent ductus arteriosus between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mosaic color mapped onto the grayscale ultrasound is color Doppler, which encodes blood flow direction and velocity. It reveals the turbulent shunt jet of a patent ductus arteriosus between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: This echocardiogram shows an aorta overriding a defect in the interventricular septum together with a thickened right ventricle. Which single diagnosis do these findings indicate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete transposition of the great arteries

explanation.summary: The study demonstrates an overriding aorta straddling a ventricular septal defect with right ventricular hypertrophy, the key anatomic features of tetralogy of Fallot; pulmonic/RVOT stenosis completes the tetrad.
explanation.whyCorrect: The study demonstrates an overriding aorta straddling a ventricular septal defect with right ventricular hypertrophy, the key anatomic features of tetralogy of Fallot; pulmonic/RVOT stenosis completes the tetrad.

questions.stem: This histologic field of inflamed pericardium shows a dense infiltrate of small cells with multilobed nuclei. Pericardial fluid analysis corresponding to this picture would most likely reveal which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lymphocyte-predominant infiltrate with normal glucose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low glucose with a high neutrophil count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clear fluid with high glucose and few cells

explanation.summary: The section shows acute purulent (neutrophil-rich) pericarditis. Bacterial purulent effusions are exudative with abundant neutrophils and characteristically low glucose, reflecting consumption by bacteria and inflammatory cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The section shows acute purulent (neutrophil-rich) pericarditis. Bacterial purulent effusions are exudative with abundant neutrophils and characteristically low glucose, reflecting consumption by bacteria and inflammatory cells.
